# Prior Art and Community Discussion

Dimension 1: does a hardware switch that cuts mount power on collision
already exist, and how does the astrophotography community talk about
camera/OTA-versus-tripod/pier collisions? Sources: [citations](../citations.md).

## Null result on the exact proposal

No source fetched in this run describes a product, patent, or reported
working build of a **contact switch on the protected device (camera/OTA)
that cuts mount DC power and stays latched until manual reset**. The
closest contact-triggered items are two suggestions, neither reported as
built:

- a pier-mounted micro switch the scope touches, wired in the mount's 12V
  line (gorann, 2025) [85];
- switches "wired into your power cord in 'normally closed'" that "cut
  power to your mount if it hits" (Cloudy Nights, 2016) [86].

All closest items are listed below. This is a null result for this source pool
(single search-engine wave, Cloudflare-blocked forums read through a
reader proxy), not proof of absence.

Items 2–5 and 8 are position- or communication-triggered, not
contact-triggered. Item 5b is position-triggered, with a later post
implying contact. Items 5a and 6 are collision-sensor proposals with no
reported build. Item 5a is the closest to the proposal, but its switch sits
on the pier rather than the payload, and its reset is not discussed. Item 1 is the closest functional match (struck switch,
hardware trip, manual recovery) but comes from one poster's recollection of
professional practice, with the poster hedging ("I think the microswitches
were push-to-break") [2].

## The December 2025 Cloudy Nights thread

A thread titled "A device to sense and prevent mount collisions?" [1], [2]
is the most direct community discussion found. Positions taken:

1. **Hardware over software.** Bob4BVM, who says he worked on professional
   safety systems: "Real protection is done with proper sensors set up to
   detect collisions... and a contactor to break the power to motor" [1];
   software hard stops are "a total violation of the fail-safe concept" [2].
   3C286 lists a hierarchy "Mechanical [best]... Electrical/Electronic...
   Software [worst]" [2]. whereIsIt points out that 3D printers use
   mechanical limit switches [2].
2. **Current sensing.** walt r proposes tripping on motor current [2];
   Bob4BVM doubts the current change is visible "with the huge gear ratios
   typical to scope drives" [2]; brebisson calls current cutoff "most likely
   the most fool proof system" [2].
3. **Sensor coverage.** ButterFly: a sensor only detects trouble at its own
   location [1]. astroneer3141: reed/magnet switches "work only for a
   particular DEC angle" [1].
4. **Reset is an open question.** momo-chan: "Does it power off the mount,
   or just stop? Recovery methods would also be necessary." [1]
5. **Bob4BVM's circuit is not fail-safe or latching as drawn (inference).**
   In [93] the trip *energizes* a relay through normally-open reed switches.
   A broken reed or coil wire therefore silently disables protection, which
   is the opposite of the NC fail-safe practice in
   [estop-requirements.md](estop-requirements.md). The circuit also
   un-trips as soon as the magnet moves off the reed. This contrasts with
   the latched, de-energize-to-trip design proposed here.
6. **False trips near legitimate motion.** iluxo notes that an ASIAIR
   meridian flip stops "approx 5 millimeters" from the tripod, so an
   accelerometer power-cut "has to pretty accurate" to avoid unnecessary
   stops. He shelved the build, citing the difficulty of training the no-go
   zone and a busy family life [1].

## Recurring community positions

1. Set limits in the mount, not only on the PC: "Only your mount knows
   where it is at, not NINA" [15]; stagger software then mount limits [15], [20].
2. Software alone is not trusted: "I wouldn't solely depend on it" [13].
3. Strain wave mounts lack the clutch slip that protects older mounts:
   "Given the torque and the lack of a clutch in strain wave mounts, it is
   very important to properly set Ra limits" [7]; "All mounts should have an
   overload cutoff" [6].
4. Hardware power cutting was already recommended in 2016: "If you're
   running remotely you need hardware safety switches" [86]. The same thread
   calls it "the type of solution used in industrial settings" [86], and
   objects that placement must change with each scope/camera configuration
   [86]. Clarkey contrasts mount types: "the GEMS just object and stop. The
   harmonic mounts just keep going" [85].
5. Cutting mount power is the robust interlock in observatories: "The mount
   won't slew if it has no power!" [10]; critical failsafes belong
   "downstream (power wise) of the controller" [8].
6. Objections to power cutting: the software session breaks [9]; a contact
   switch fires only after contact [11]; sensors give false readings [11].
   Both [11] quotes come from a roll-off-roof thread and are applied here by
   analogy.

## Gaps and Limitations

- SGL 436714 page 3 was supplied by the operator [85]. Clarkey's build
  turns the mount off, but his power path and reset are only in a wiring
  diagram posted in the SGL DIY section, which was not reached.
- Bob4BVM's attached schematic [93] was fetched as an image. The topology
  in [93] is a transcription of a drawing, not source text.
- SGL 246307 [92] turned out to be about dome homing, not mount protection.
  CN 959669 was not reached.
- Facebook groups and Discord were not reachable.
- Patent search was limited to what turned up in web results. No dedicated
  patent database search was done.
